This rock is almost two billion years old.
The canyon around it is only five or six million.
So how does one river cut a mile into solid rock, that fast?
With grit. The Colorado River carries sand, gravel and even boulders, and in floods they scour the riverbed like sandpaper.
But grit only cuts when the water is fast, and fast water needs a steep drop to the sea.
Long before the canyon, the ground here was pushed up thousands of feet into a high, flat plateau. So when the river found its way to the sea, it had a steep drop, and it cut straight down.
As it cut, it opened up a stack of old worlds: seabeds, swamps, and a desert of sand dunes, frozen into a cliff.
Hard layers stand as cliffs. Soft ones crumble into slopes, so the walls step down like a staircase.
But the river mostly cuts down. The width comes from side canyons: flash floods and rockfall after rockfall, pulling the walls up to 18 miles apart.
So the land rose, the river fell fast, its grit ground a mile down, and the side canyons pulled the walls apart.
And it's not finished. Floods still cut, and the walls still fall.
